note:
FILER'S CORRECTION — read this BEFORE designing the fix. It demotes the framing in the task body.

I filed this task's body before enumerating the dispatch window on #2054. That
enumeration changes the diagnosis materially.

WHAT THE BODY SAYS: the owner-blind terminate guard is the primary gap — a
non-owner can self-post the upload-verification PASS and destroy a live owner's
pod, and nothing in the surface catches it.

WHAT IS ACTUALLY TRUE: the surface DID carry the catch, and it was skipped.
`spec-ladder-2054` posted a `[long-phase-heartbeat]` on #2054 at 19:27:39Z
reading, verbatim: "pod=pod-2054-tiers pilot PASS ... Production launched
19:26Z ... fence re-sized to 2x = 4 h (alarm ~23:30Z) ... launcher pid 1763."
That is an explicit live-owner declaration with an unexpired fence, sitting in
the durable record two hours before the 21:32:37Z teardown. The pre-dispatch
external-marker triage duty (SKILL.md Step 9 entry guard) is exactly the
mechanism that surfaces such a marker, and the orchestrator skipped it — the
watcher's triage-observer had already flagged the same omission twice earlier
the same day (17:33:03Z, 19:53:02Z) before flagging the 22:11:10Z dispatch.

REVISED SCOPE — do NOT over-build:
  - PRIMARY failure was execution discipline against an EXISTING duty. No new
    detection mechanism is required to have prevented this incident. Resist
    designing one.
  - The owner-blind guard is a REAL but SECONDARY defense-in-depth gap: a
    correctly-triaged non-owner could still terminate, because
    `_guard_upload_verification_before_terminate` asks only whether some PASS
    marker with an `outroot=` token exists, never who owns the pod, while
    CLAUDE.md scopes the grant to "the agent actively driving a job on a pod it
    provisioned" in prose no code reads.
  - Therefore prefer the SMALLEST change that closes the secondary gap. The
    highest-value single check is fence-awareness: refuse (or require an
    explicit override) when the task carries an owner heartbeat/fence whose
    deadline is in the FUTURE. Note the shape carefully — a fence is OLD by
    construction and still binding, so the #2111 pre-stop probe's
    "breadcrumb younger than ~10 min" recency test structurally cannot detect
    it. Recency is the wrong predicate here; deadline-in-future is the right one.
  - Body items 2 (owner attribution on the PASS) and 3 (non-owner surface-for-
    approval path) remain reasonable but are lower priority than item 1, and
    should not grow into a general ownership-tracking subsystem.
  - Body item 4 stands unchanged: add conditions, never remove the existing
    upload-verification or `outroot=` (#2187) checks.

A cheap, high-value companion worth considering in the same round: make the
triage-observer's finding HARDER TO IGNORE for repeat offences on the same task
within a session — three identical flags in one day on #2054 produced no
behaviour change. That is a surfacing-strength question, not a new detector.

NO DATA WAS LOST in the incident: uploads were complete (113/113 verified
independently), teardown went through the gated path with `outroot=swept-clean`,
and the owner's own re-merge confirmed byte-equality with the harvested commit.
The benign outcome owed to clean uploads, not to the mechanism.
